name: Acamprosate (Campral)
summary: A medication used to support continued abstinence in people with alcohol use disorder.
description: Acamprosate is a synthetic amino acid derivative that helps normalize the imbalance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) signaling that develops after long-term alcohol use. By modulating glutamatergic transmission, it reduces the brain hyperexcitability associated with early abstinence.
patient_summary: Acamprosate is a medicine for people who have already stopped drinking and want help staying sober. It can lessen the physical drive to drink and make it easier to maintain abstinence over time.

linked_conditions.context: Used to maintain abstinence after detoxification.

contraindications: Severe renal impairment (CrCl 30 mL/min or less)

efficacy_response.patient_text: Across studies, about 36 out of 100 people taking acamprosate remained completely sober for 6 months, compared with about 23 out of 100 people taking a placebo (sugar pill).

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Acamprosate is used to help people with alcohol use disorder stay abstinent after they have already stopped drinking. It is not used to manage withdrawal or to help someone cut down while still drinking heavily.
items: Maintenance of abstinence in {link:condition:alcohol-use-disorder:alcohol use disorder} after detoxification is complete and abstinence is achieved.
sections.patient_text: This medication is meant for people who have already gone through detox and stopped drinking. It is used to help them stay alcohol-free and is not useful if someone is still drinking regularly.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone responds differently, but these are common experiences people report while taking acamprosate after they stop drinking:

quotes: The urge to drink is still there sometimes, but it feels more distant and easier to say no.
I still think about alcohol, but it doesn’t feel as powerful or overwhelming.
It didn’t magically erase cravings, but it took the edge off enough for therapy and meetings to really help.
items.note: Acamprosate usually reduces the intensity and frequency of cravings rather than eliminating them completely.

quotes: My body felt less on edge—less jittery and wired all the time.
Sleep and mood slowly felt more stable as the weeks went on.
Early recovery still felt hard, but my baseline felt more steady.
The diarrhea was annoying the first week but settled down after a while.
I had some trouble sleeping at first, but it evened out.
Overall it felt pretty "neutral"—I mostly noticed it when I forgot a dose.
items.note: Diarrhea is the most common side effect. Many people find it improves over time or with dose adjustments.

quotes: I’m not sure how much was the medicine versus meetings and therapy.
I didn’t feel anything dramatic, but I also didn’t relapse, so I stayed on it.
It’s more like a quiet support in the background than a noticeable “buzz” or high.

sections.heading: Onset and Duration of Benefit
sections.text: Clinical benefit generally emerges within about 5–8 days of starting treatment, with effects maintained as long as therapy continues and abstinence is supported.
key_points: Clinical benefit often begins within 5–8 days after starting acamprosate.
Full effect may take several weeks of sustained abstinence and regular dosing.
Benefits are maintained only while the medication is continued and alcohol use remains minimal or absent.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: A meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials found that 36% of patients treated with acamprosate maintained continuous abstinence at 6 months, compared with 23.4% of those receiving placebo. The benefit is modest but clinically important when combined with behavioral treatment.
sections.clinical_details: Rösner et al. (2010) analyzed multiple randomized controlled trials of acamprosate for alcohol dependence. Across studies, acamprosate was associated with a significantly higher rate of continuous abstinence at 6 months (36% vs 23.4% with placebo), with the greatest benefits seen when combined with psychosocial interventions.
sections.patient_text: In research studies, people taking acamprosate were more likely to stay completely alcohol-free for 6 months than those taking a placebo—36% versus 23.4%. It is most helpful when used together with counseling or support programs.

citation.label: Rösner S, et al. Acamprosate for alcohol dependence. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010

sections.heading: Warnings & Precautions
sections.highlight: Monitor mood closely, especially in early recovery, and avoid using acamprosate as a substitute for comprehensive alcohol use disorder treatment.
other: Monitor mood closely; may be associated with worsening depression or suicidal thoughts in some patients.
Not effective in individuals who continue to drink heavily or have not yet achieved abstinence.
Does not relieve or prevent the symptoms of acute alcohol withdrawal.
Should always be integrated into a broader treatment plan that includes psychosocial interventions (e.g., counseling, mutual support groups).
patient_counseling: Let your clinician know right away if you feel more depressed, hopeless, or have thoughts of harming yourself.
You need to be abstinent before starting acamprosate; this medicine does not treat withdrawal and will not help you safely stop alcohol on your own.
If you slip and drink, do not stop the medication on your own—talk with your treatment team. Acamprosate is often continued to support getting back to sobriety.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The most common side effect is diarrhea, which is usually mild to moderate and often improves over time. Mood changes and sleep disturbance can also occur and should be monitored.
plain_language_list: Diarrhea (most common side effect, about 1 in 6 people)

common.patient_note: This is the most common side effect, affecting roughly 1 in 6 people.

serious: Suicidal ideation or tendencies (monitor mood closely).
CNS depression or impairment (caution with driving and operating machinery until effects are known).

sections.heading: Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Acamprosate is renally excreted and not metabolized by the liver, so it has very few pharmacokinetic drug interactions compared with many other medications used in alcohol use disorder.

items.risk: Continued alcohol use can blunt the medication’s benefit on abstinence.
items.action: Avoid alcohol to get the full benefit of treatment.

items.risk: Minimal, as acamprosate is not metabolized hepatically.
items.action: No major cytochrome P450–related precautions are needed, but always review your full medication list with your prescriber.

sections.heading: Tapering & Discontinuation
sections.text: Acamprosate is not associated with physiological dependence, so it can typically be stopped without tapering. Clinical follow-up is still important, as stopping may affect relapse risk.
key_points: Acamprosate does not produce physical dependence or a withdrawal syndrome when stopped.
A formal taper is usually not required; however, abrupt discontinuation may still increase relapse risk if support is not in place.
Discuss any plan to stop acamprosate with your clinician so that your overall relapse-prevention plan can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Dosing & Administration
sections.text: Dosing is weight- and kidney-function–sensitive. Standard dosing is three times daily, and tablets should be swallowed whole.

adult.notes: Lower doses (333 or 666 mg two times daily) may be considered in patients weighing less than 60 kg. Tablets should be swallowed whole; do not crush or chew.

sections.patient_text: The usual dose is 666 mg three times a day, often taken as two 333 mg tablets, three times daily. Take the tablets whole with fluid—do not crush or chew them. People with lower body weight may be prescribed a smaller dose.

renal_adjustments.patient_note: If your kidneys do not work as well, your doctor will prescribe a lower dose.
If you have severe kidney disease, this medicine is not considered safe for you.

hepatic_adjustments.condition: Mild to moderate (Child-Pugh A or B)

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Use acamprosate cautiously in special populations, with particular attention to renal function and the limited data available in pregnancy and lactation.
sections.pregnancy: Use only if the potential benefit justifies the possible risk to the fetus (often classified as Category C).
sections.lactation: It is not clear whether acamprosate passes into breast milk; use cautiously and consider the risks and benefits with the patient.
sections.pediatrics: Safety and efficacy have not been established in children and adolescents; not recommended.
sections.geriatrics: Dosage should be adjusted according to renal function, which often declines with age.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Renal function at baseline and periodically, especially in older adults or those with known kidney disease.
Ongoing alcohol use and adherence to the medication regimen.
Mood symptoms and suicidality, particularly during early recovery.
Engagement in psychosocial treatment (counseling, mutual support groups, recovery programs).

sections.heading: Dosage Forms & Strengths
sections.text: Acamprosate is formulated for oral use in enteric-coated tablets.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Acamprosate appears to stabilize the imbalance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmission that occurs in chronic alcohol exposure, in part by decreasing activity at NMDA-type glutamate receptors. This reduces the hyperglutamatergic state associated with early abstinence.

image.alt: Diagram of GABA and Glutamate receptors in the brain

sections.patient_text: Long-term drinking leaves the brain in an overexcited state. Acamprosate helps quiet those overactive signals and support the brain’s calming systems, which can reduce physical cravings. It does not treat alcohol withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: Clinical Pearls & Place in Treatment
sections.text: Acamprosate works best when started soon after detoxification and combined with structured psychosocial treatment, such as counseling or mutual support groups. It is not indicated for managing acute alcohol withdrawal, where benzodiazepines remain the mainstay. Because acamprosate is not metabolized by the liver and is renally excreted, it is often preferred in patients with significant liver disease but adequate kidney function.

items.label: Rösner S, et al. Acamprosate for alcohol dependence. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010

faqs.a: Acamprosate is prescribed to help people with alcohol use disorder stay abstinent after they have stopped drinking. It supports long-term sobriety but is not a treatment for acute withdrawal symptoms.

faqs.q: Do I need to stop drinking before starting Acamprosate?
faqs.a: Yes. You should already be sober before starting acamprosate. It does not help you get through withdrawal safely and is not effective if you are still drinking regularly.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking Acamprosate?
faqs.a: Drinking alcohol while on acamprosate may undermine the medication’s benefits and increase the risk of relapse. For best results, avoid alcohol completely and use this medication as part of a structured recovery plan that includes counseling and support.

faqs.q: How effective is Acamprosate at helping people stay sober?
faqs.a: In clinical trials, around 36% of people taking acamprosate remained completely abstinent for 6 months, compared with about 23.4% taking a placebo. While it is not a guarantee, it modestly improves the chances of maintaining sobriety when combined with psychosocial treatment.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Acamprosate when stopping it?
faqs.a: No taper is usually required because acamprosate does not cause physical dependence. However, you should still talk with your clinician before stopping, since changes in medication may affect your relapse risk and overall treatment plan.
